speechtext:
In connection with this Bill No. 3, I listened with interest to the evidence which was given by various officials of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and other organizations. The point which came to my mind was that the evidence to which we listened was largely that of the running trades. If this bill were passed it would mean that all new employees of the railways would have to be bilingual. It would mean that all employees, including extra gangs and men engaged in maintenance of way and other works, would have to be bilingual. It would affect seriously many men in the province who have not the advantage of knowing both languages. In my constituency there are men of both nationalities and I have found that a great many of them are not bilingual. A great many of them are employed as labourers and they can speak only one language. The effect would be injurious there. While the majority of the people in my constituency are English-speaking, in some of the crews the men are as high as eighty per cent Frenchspeaking. For that reason, while I am in sympathy with the bill I feel it is not right that we should give to the transport board the authority which is sought in the bill.
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops):	I have
the highest regard for the mover of this bill and I do not believe that anyone in the house will question either his sincerity or his motives. I am of the opinion that to discuss a question of this sort is in the interests of the people. It makes no difference whether we agree with the bill or not, this motion gives every hon. member an opportunity to state his opinion and it brings out facts that we had not known before. May I quote the underlined words in the bill:
.	.	. providing for the employment in the
province of Quebec of employees duly qualified in the knowledge and use of the language of the majority of the citizens of such province requisite to the performance of their duties.
That gives a great deal of latitude to the transport board. The first business of any great transportation company is to provide transportation and service that will be satisfactory to the people, and if they cannot do that in Quebec because the employees are not versed in the language of the province, then they are not giving such service to the people.
The railways themselves are opposed, not to the principle of the bill but to its provisions which will set up restrictions to be imposed upon the railways. For that reason they are opposed to it. The labour organizations, at least those in the running trades,

engineers, firemen, trainmen and conductors, are opposed to it also, on the ground that it will interfere with long-standing seniority rights. There are a great many people who are of opinion that the labour organizations are so strong that they hold a club over the heads of the railway companies, and that the companies are objecting to the bill because of pressure put upon them by these organizations. That is absolutely wrong; it is not in accordance with the facts. Seniority holds good only so long as a man can discharge the duties required of him, and when he cannot do so the labour organizations do not insist upon his retaining his position on account of seniority.
I make these statements in order to remove any misundei-standing there may be with respect to seniority and the power the labour organizations have under the rule. There is another point with regard to the briefs submitted by the railway labour organizations. The labour organizations say that arbitrarily to place in the railway service in the province of Quebec only employees who are conversant with the French language would impose a hardship on the other employees. Some people have taken exception to this because they say that is not what the bill calls for. But that is exactly what the bill calls for-bilingualism. Because the labour organizations object to employing "in the province of Quebec, only employees who are conversant with the French language,'' it is assumed that they are referring to employees who are conversant with the French language only. But there is a difference between the phrases "only employees who are conversant with the French language" and "employees who are conversant with the French language only." The latter is the construction which some people have put upon the brief submitted by the railway organizations, but that construction is wrong.
In view of the fact that the labour organizations and the railway companies are opposed to the bill-not to the principle of the bill but to the privileges that will be extended to the transport board-I suggest that the house would be ill advised to proceed with it.

speechtext:
This bill amends a very important act, perhaps one of the most important on the statute books of Canada, the Railway Act. In amending an important act of this kind it behooves the department responsible for the administration of that act to make very sure that the proposed amendment is sound legislation. No one, in considering this legislation in relation to the act that it amends, can say that it is good legislation.

Railway Act*-Language Requirement
The Railway Act applies to every province of Canada. This amendment singles out one province for special treatment. It does not say that the employees in all the provinces shall speak the language of the majority of the people with whom they come in contact; it provides that only in the province of Quebec must that rule hold true. That, I submit, is not the proper type of amendment to apply to an act drawn to govern all parts of Canada.
It might be thought that the bill as applying to the province of Quebec would affect only railway employees in that province. If the terms of the bill were to be carried out literally by the transport board, its effect would extend far beyond the boundaries of Quebec. The city of Montreal is the great railway centre of Canada. From Montreal trains go to western Canada over the southern route and also over the northern route; trains go to the maritime provinces, to the New England states and in the direction of New York city. All these trains would necessarily be affected outside the province of Quebec, because running crews are not changed at the provincial boundaries, they must operate from Montreal considerably beyond' the boundaries of the province. Therefore the effect of this bill would be far wider than a simple reading of it might suggest. Of course I think no one will challenge the statement that it is highly desirable that employees on trains should speak the language of all the people with whom they come in contact. Without doubt bilingualism is very desirable in Quebec province. But what would be the effect of this bill on the railway employee with many years of seniority who is not bilingual? That man could never look for promotion, I think if the provisions of the bill were applied literally he could hardly be certain of his employment.
The seniority rules of the railways are of tremendous value both to the employees and to the management; they have grown up over a period of years; they are administered to-day almost automatically and without disturbance either to the employees, organizations or to the management. Certainly those rules of seniority would become a dead letter if this bill were enacted and applied. That, I believe, would be a serious calamity both for the employees and for the railways.
When this bill was referred to the committee it was for the purpose of enabling all interested parties to appear and give evidence. It is worthy of remark that all those who came before the committee testified that the bill was bad legislation and would not improve the situation so far as the lailways or their employees or the employees of the other
utilities which it is the intention of the provisions of the bill to reach are concerned. The chairman of the committee has told us that each of the railways was represented before the committee and gave evidence to the effect that this legislation is undesirable. Evidence was given that both railways have endeavoured to promote bilingualism among their employees, in Quebec province, and that considerable advance has been made in that direction.
Some comment has been made in this debate that the Canadian Pacific has made greater advances in this direction than the Canadian National. If that is true, as it quite well may be, I would recall to hon. members that the Canadian National did not grow up as the Canadian National system, but that it is a consolidation of a number of lines, some of which operated only to a small extent in the province of Quebec. For instance, the Grand Trunk Railway had its terminal in Montreal but had only a small mileage in Quebec province. Similarly the Canadian Northern operated into Montreal but had only a small mileage in Quebec. Trains from the Intercolonial railway passed into the terminal at Montreal, but of course the Intercolonial did not previously have any considerable mileage in Quebec. Therefore the Canadian National Railways have had a much shorter time to promote bilingualism among their employees than the Canadian Pacific. I feel quite certain that the management of the Canadian National are just as zealous in their efforts to promote bilingualism as is the Canadian Pacific. I know that when vacancies occur in the province of Quebec every effort is made to bring forward bilingual operators to fill those positions. I know that on the Canadian National the demand for bilingual employees is much in excess of the supply. For the senior positions on the railway experience is needed and seniority is needed. Unfortunately 'the supply of senior men who are bilingual is not as great as could be desired. The only way to correct this would be to disregard the seniority list, simply drop back the older employees who are not bilingual and bring on young men over their heads.
As I said, there is no question as to general agreement with the purpose of this bill; whether we reside in Quebec or not, we all agree it is highly desirable that operators in that province be bilingual. But to call on the board of transport commissioners to take steps to see that this is brought about within any short length of time would, I think, be imposing on the board a task that they could

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lawson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was drawing attention to the fact that the difficulty which faces the people of this country did not arise because of any lack of capital goods, but was largely a matter of maldistribution or uneven distribution of the national income. On the need for the investment of new capital the minister had this to say in his budget speech, as reported on pege 3143 of Hansard:
If we can no longer count on great possibilities of expansion extensively by pushing back farther the borders of settlement or by means of a rapid growth in population, then we must expand intensively by improving our capital equipment, by making ours a better rather than a bigger country. On the frontiers of science, invention and technology the possibilities of expansion are greater than they ever were on the geographical frontier.
If that means anything at all, it means that if we are going to keep on investing capital we shall have to do it by improving the capital structure that we already have, making it more perfect and more efficient. There is nothing said about increasing consumption. There is nothing said about devising ways and means by which the Canadian people may benefit from an increase in producers' goods. Then the minister continued at page 3143:
However, in order .to expand production, employment and incomes, we must have substantially more capital creation, a more rapid rate of private investment. Someone must convert a larger proportion of the savings of the people into capital expenditures or else our national income will decline again. Look back on 'tihe history of this or other countries in their modern phase and you will find prosperity only with expansion, only when the people were busy creating new capital works. In our prosperous first _ decade of this century we were busy extending our capital equipment, building cities, railways, harbours, elevators and factories.
[Mr. Howe.l
That is all true, Mr. Speaker, but the trouble is that we have built too many railways, too many harbours, too many elevators and warehouses which are now empty and some of which have scarcely ever been used. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) wants us to go on and produce more of those things, in order that we may have still more monuments standing to our inefficiency and muddling. Then he continues:
In our post-war period of prosperity, from 1925 to 1930, we were busy building houses, factories, power plants, roads and automobiles. Since that time, 'investment in durable goods has languished. It revived somewhat in 1936 and 1937, particularly in the mining industry, and persisted well into 1938, with some recession thereafter. But it is still very far below the levels needed .to utilize fully our increased labour and other resources. Its full recovery is our greatest need to-day.
If the need is for capital goods, will someone tell me why our warehouses are full of things our people need and cannot buy? And if we double our production of durable goods, is there any assurance that we will double our production of consumer goods; and if we do not, are we any better off than we were before? I ask the Minister of Finance and other hon. members in all seriousness if ever again they expect to see an expansion in Canada equal to that which took place between 1900 and 1929. If the answer is yes, then I would ask them on what they base their expectation. What is the material basis for their hope? I do not think any intelligent person who has given thought to the matter can have any such expectation.
I can understand the viewpoint of the Minister of Finance. It is the orthodox economist's viewpoint. He holds to the theory that the prime purpose of capital goods is to produce capital. That is the theory of capitalism-that its purpose is the production of more and more capital, not the production of human goods and human requirements; these are only incidental. The production of capital goods is not an end in itself. The man who made the first hoe did not make it in order that he might continue making hoes. He made it in order to enable him to till the soil better, in order to get a greater return from it so that he might live better. Therefore the investment in capital goods is merely a means to an end; that is, it is a means to enable us to provide ourselves with our everyday needs in consumers' goods and services. That being the case, surely the time must arrive when we shall have all the durable goods we require or, if not, when our production of durable goods will be much less than when we began building our capital structure.

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
I submit that time is here now, and what we need to encourage is not the production of more durable goods but the production and distribution of consumers' goods. Does the minister think we can go on forever expanding our frontiers-and I think he will agree that is now completed-or go on building and improving our capital structure without in some way and by some means increasing the share of that production which goes to the producers in industry?
On Sunday last the President of the United States opened the New York world's fair. In the report of his speech which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 1, I find the following:	.
In declaring the fair "open to all mankind" the president paid tribute to the foresight of the nation's early leaders. He said they successfully planned a constitution to fit it to a constantly expanding nation.
The fact that the original framework was capable of expansion from its application to thirteen states with less than 4,000,000 people to forty-eight states with more than 130,000,000 he said stood "unique in the whole history of the world, for no other form of government has remained unchanged so long and seen, at the same time, any comparable expansion of population or of area."
The point to which I wish to draw attention is that somewhere about 1776, when the constitution of the United States was drawn up, the population of the United States was only a few million-of course more than the
4.000.	000 mentioned by the president, but not very much more. Yet during that period of about one hundred and sixty years they have conquered a whole continent, turned a whole continent of virgin forest and primeval prairie into a country teeming with cities, towns and cultivated farms, with a population of
130.000.	000 people. That time has passed. The capital and labour that were expended on the building and expansion of the nation must now be used for the betterment and welfare of mankind, so that the people will be able to take advantage of the great progress made by the science, invention and technology to which the minister referred.
But supposing the action proposed in the budget does result in increased expenditures on durable goods; what will be the result? For a short period during the year in which buildings and extensions to buildings and plants are under construction, employment will increase, and demands for consumers' goods will also increase. For a time conditions will be better. But as the new factories come into production with the best and most up-to-the-minute labour-saving machinery, workers will be dismissed, because the machines will be doing the workers' work.
Unemployment will increase and consumers' demands will again decrease. The national income will be increased, but the share of that national income going to the workers will be relatively less, while the share going to the owners of capital will be relatively greater because of the efficiency of the new equipment. This has been the history of capitalistic development since it first began. It is a fact that our capacity to produce continually outstrips our capacity to consume, and this keeps our productive system in a chronic state of depression.
In the golden age referred to by the Minister of Finance, from 1925 to 1930, nearly half the manufacturing effort of Canada was devoted to the output of producer goods. This was at the height of the so-called Canadian prosperity, and yet only a little more than one-half of our manufacturing effort was devoted to the production of consumer goods. Evidently there was a lack of balance between the two forms of production. In any event, the boom, which was based largely on the production of capital goods, collapsed. The result was that Canada found itself with a huge amount of capital equipment facilities for producing, transporting and storing consumer goods which it could not consume. I remember hearing the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, make the statement in this house, I think it was in 1934 or 1935, that at that time Canada had sufficient equipment to provide for a population of
25,000,000, and we had a population of only some 10,500,000. Yet the Minister of Finance tells us that what we need is more capital goods to produce other goods that we cannot consume.
It is evident that the production of capital goods at that time defeated its own end; that is, if its end was the production of consumer welfare. The value of investment in capital goods shrank, and in many instances vanished entirely. The equipment duplication of capital is a serious fault of the present system. It spells waste and inefficiency on every hand. Because of the hope that new capital equipment may prove the means of increased exploitation, the urge to produce is powerful, almost irresistible. This is nearly always the case, unless in a given industry control has reached the monopolistic stage. In that event the capital is kept down to the requirements of the existing market. The over-production of capital equipment in this period between 1925 and 1930 meant the diversion of manufacturing effort which might better have been applied to the production of consumer goods. If it were only possible

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
to do that under a profit economy, the production of consumer goods might well have been doubled with a corresponding increase in the standard of living. But that is something which cannot take place as long as we are living under a profit economy. I have before me an index of industrial activity which appeared in the April, 1939, monthly letter of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. This is what they say:
The general level of industrial activity in Canada, as measured by this bank's index, has remained virtually unchanged from mid-January to mid-March, factories and other industrial plants continuing to operate at 69 per cent of capacity and at 84 per cent of 1937 activity.
Many industries did not reach that high level of 69 per cent capacity. The production of food, drink and tobacco in March was only 57 per cent of capacity; clothing, textiles and shoes was 87 per cent; pulp and paper, 66 per cent; wood products, 77 per cent; automotive trades, 75 per cent; iron and steel, 52 per cent. This item is divided into heavy, medium and light and 52 per cent is the average. The point I wish to make is that with our present capital plant we are not operating at anything approaching capacity. In a book published a few years ago by Howard Henry Pratt Fairchild, professor of sociology, I think in the university of New York, he quotes H. L. Gantt who, he says, is one of the foremost efficiency engineers in the United States. This gentleman states that, on the whole, only about 50 per cent of industrial machines are actually operating during the time they are expected to operate, and, on the whole, during the time they are being operated, they are producing only about 50 per cent of what they are expected to produce. This brings our productive result down to about one-fourth of what it might be if our machines were run all the time at their highest capacity.
It is true that we were relatively prosperous during our periods of expansion; at least some were prosperous and most of the others hoped to be. But as I pointed out in this house a few days ago, that period is over. As I also pointed out, I do not see why that should be any reason for our living in poverty and in the deep gloom which evidently enshrouded the Minister of Finance when he was preparing his budget speech. If we cannot produce producer goods, we can produce consumer goods. That, indeed, should be the real purpose for any expenditure on capital goods. In an orderly society where the common good was the purpose of productive effort there would be rejoicing, and not despair, 
when it was ascertained at last that the building of the capital structure was finished. We could then go on with the production of consumer goods of all kinds and reap the reward that we have waited for so long. But not so under the present system where the ability to provide ourselves with an abundance of goods and services fills us with gloom and dismay. So, Mr. Speaker, I do not see that any value will come to the people of Canada through the proposal made by the Minister of Finance that income used for capital purposes should be exempted from income tax.
I wish now to say a word on another matter. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) upon his political progress. It is no mean distance that he has travelled when he can bring himself to the point where he is willing to vote for a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment, and against his own party. I do hope that he will persevere with his study and investigation of the principles upon which our platform is based. I am sure, if he does that, he will come to the conclusion that there is only one way in which one can live a truly Christian life, and that is by forswearing forever a system that continues to exist by exploitation of the widow and the fatherless.
I should like also to advise him that there are more reliable sources of information as to our program and policies than even Cardinal Villeneuve, whom the hon. member for Humboldt quoted last evening. Perhaps the hon. member does not know that we published a reply to Cardinal Villeneuve's statement. Part of the cardinal's statement which the hon. member read into the record last night reads as follows:
The C.C.F. program contains several fundamental errors. Let me very briefly describe the first error in the C.C.F. program which advocates the suppression or at least the quasisuppression of private property. Now the right to own property is not derived from human laws but from nature, and every man has by nature the right to possess property as his own.
The abolition of private ownership leads to state ownership and therefore the C.C.F. program proposes the nationalization of practically all forms of industry and other means of production and state ownership of all financial companies, etc.
In this evening's paper I read that three hundred young men in this city last night did not have so much private property as to afford them a place to sleep. They had neither private nor public property. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has not yet been in office in this country, so it cannot be held responsible for that state of affairs. Nevertheless that is the state of affairs of an increas-

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
ing number of people in this country, who are being deprived of every vestige of private property. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman), addressing the house yesterday, referred to the fact that eighty per cent of the farmers of this country had not bought a new suit of clothes during the last eight years. He stated that fifty per cent of our farmers were bankrupt and seventy-five per cent of Canadian farms were mortgaged. I should like to know who it was that despoiled these people. Who deprived them of their property? It could not have been the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation because we have not had that opportunity. Cardinal Villeneuve had better look elsewhere for those who are depriving the people of private property.

speechtext: Read the rest of the statement which the hon. member for Humboldt quoted.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no objection to reading it all. I have read the last part of it; the first paragraph reads as follows:
Now I will deal with my attitude towards the C.C.F. One of the principal leaders of the C.C.F. declared that their program was based on frankly socialist principles. That is true; the C.C.F. and communism, economic programs are practically the same. The only difference is that the communists admit that they are prepared to attain their object by violent means, while the C.C.F. think they will accomplish their purpose peacefully.
The late pope issued an encyclical

the Encyclical Quadragesimo Anno-in which, speaking of our present capitalist system, he had this to say, which is not very much different from what I have been saying in this house for many years:
You assuredly know . . . and you lament the ultimate consequence of this individualistic spirit in economic affairs. Free competition is dead.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) made a similar statement this afternoon. The encyclical continues:
Economic dictatorship has taken its place.
Unbridled ambition for domination has succeeded the desire for gain; the whole economic life has become hard, cruel and relentless in a ghastly measure.
I quote another paragraph from the encyclical:
For it is rightly contended that certain forms of property must be reserved to the state, since they carry with them an opportunity of domination too great to be left to private .individuals without injury to the community at large.
May I say that it has not yet been decided to what extent, in the interests of the public, in the interests of the common man and the 71492-218
comman woman, it will be necessary to socialize the means of production. Much is being done cooperatively already'.
I should like now to draw the attention of the hon. member for Humboldt, and of others who may care to hear it, to the fact that the principles and program of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are in complete harmony with the programs of the labour and socialist movements in such countries as Great Britain, Sweden and New Zealand. In New Zealand the prime minister and four members of his labour government are Roman Catholics. Of the British labour party the late Cardinal Bourne said:
It Should be recognized that the British Labour party, although calling itself socialist, does not fall within that category of socialist schools of thought condemned by His Holiness. I do not hesitate to say that Catholics are free to support and become members of the British socialist movement.
I should like to show hon. members how private monopoly is despoiling the people of this country and making inevitable the conditions that we have to-day. A few years ago there sat in these very buildings what was known as the price spreads and mass buying committee, which was later continued in the form of a royal commission. It investigated a number of industries in Canada and in almost every one, if not all, of the industries investigated, the committee found two things: (1) ruthless exploitation of the workers in industry', and (2) ruthless exploitation of the consumer as well. As my time is passing I shall take just a moment to refer to one industry which was investigated, the tobacco industry.
In 1933 there were over one hundred tobacco firms doing business in Canada-127 to be exact. One firm controlled 70 per cent of the production, and another firm handled most of the remaining 30 per cent. According to the report of the mass buying commission the net profits of the larger of these tobacco companies for the five years, 1929 to 1933, amounted to S36.000.000, dividends rose from the usual rate of 7 per cent to 10^ per cent. Bear in mind that this increase in the dividend rate occurred during the three years when the depression was at its worst. But that was not all by any means. During those same hard years, when the great majority of the people of Canada were undergoing unprecedented hardships, the president of this company was drawing a salary of $25,000 a year, with annual bonuses which in some years ran as high as $60,000, and the vice-president was drawing a salary of $40,000 a year, with annual bonuses which in some

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

years ran as high as $102,000. These men can buy many suits of clothes on those salaries. They are not at all in the position of the farmers mentioned by the hon. member for Carle ton yesterday.
I could go on and on. During those years the company not only increased its dividend but cut in about half the price of raw tobacco to the growers; it also reduced the wages of its employees in both factories and stores. The average wage in the tobacco factories in 1934 was $11.25 a week, or $585 a year. Compare that with the $85,000 and the $142,000 yearly received by tobacco company officials. But there is something even worse than that. The president of the other large tobacco company was at this time drawing an annual salary of $260,000. If you compare that with the average annual salary of $585 drawn by workers in the tobacco factories, you will find that the average worker would have to live and work for 446 years to get as much as the president got in one year. And yet it is said that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is going to take away the property of the people! Almost all the property of the people is already taken away, and unless such a policy as ours is adopted it will all be taken away. Only by adopting a program such as we suggest can the people have private property and live happy, decent, Christian lives.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The annual budget debate affords an opportunity for each member of parliament to offer a few remarks, and I am going to avail myself of that opportunity. My first words are congratulations to the minister who delivered the budget speech upon the fact that his health has apparently been restored. I am sure that in offering congratulations to him I am speaking not only for myself but for my constituents.
My next word is a tribute of gratitude and praise to the present government. There is no doubt that it has enacted some beneficial legislation. That fact should be recognized by all good Canadians. Chief among these enactments, in my opinion, are the two trade treaties with the United States, one in 1935, the other in 1938. If I were to pick out one item which I believe will be more beneficial than any other, I would say that the outstanding feature of the agreement is the concession granted to our cattle raisers, although there is no doubt that people generally throughout the country will receive benefits.
I deem it a great privilege to stand here, a farmer member, speaking in the interests of the people of my constituency. I do not want

to appear sectional. This country belongs to Canadians, and while sometimes we from the west may seem to stress our own difficulties and problems compared with those of other parts of Canada, it is because of the fact that we are in circumstances of extreme difficulty.
It was not always thus. There was a time when western Canadians could hold up their heads, put their hands in their pockets and pay their bills along with any man or woman in Canada, but that time seems to have faded. We now have the spectacle, among two and a half million western Canadians in the prairie provinces and British Columbia, of 300,000 farmers who are almost at their wits' end to know how they will meet their next payment. It is well for this house to remember that, in years gone by, hundreds of millions of dollars of new wealth was created in the west. It was dug from the top six inches of the soil and it is capable of being reproduced from year to year. This prairie land was pioneered by the inhabitants of the older provinces and it is now occupied by their descendants.
I believe it is a fact that the growing of wheat is Canada's greatest industry, and I think it will continue to be so for a long time to come. We have heard the expression that the plains of western Canada are the granary of the empire. I do not think that statement can be gainsaid, although we know that other portions of the British empire can produce a great deal of grain. The prairie provinces have contributed a great deal to the dominion. They have afforded an opportunity to establish homes to large numbers of men and women who were bom and raised in other parts of the country. They have provided opportunities for the investment of capital. They have expanded our transportation facilities, with all that this means to the labour and industry of Canada. They have been the cause of the establishment of huge factories in eastern Canada to take care of our needs. All of this, Mr. Speaker, I maintain, was a splendid contribution, and I know it is recognized in other parts of the dominion.
I intended to refer to the wheat marketing problem, but as that subject is almost taboo at the present time I shall make no more than an observation. We understand that legislation is pending and that we shall have an opportunity to speak more fully on the subject when that legislation comes down. The people of western Canada were grateful to the present government when they guaranteed them an initial price of 80 cents a bushel for last year's wheat crop. I believe that our people are justified in their demand

The Budget-Mr. Leader
that this 80-cent initial price shall continue for this year's crop. All I want to say regarding this matter is that I support whole-heartedly the western delegation which made that proposal here over a month ago; I have not wavered in the slightest from that position.
We have heard a great deal about the tariff and how it bears upon the people of Canada. Some people say they are tired of the subject. Some doubt whether it has had a detrimental effect in various parts of the country. But it seems to me that we in the west have a perfect right to discuss this question because we are the ones who, through lack of factories and the difficulties of marketing our products, have to bear the greatest part of the tariff burden. This opinion is generally held. A foremost advocate in the west of a reduction in the tariff to relieve the situation is that great Liberal paper, the Winnipeg Free Press. I will not quote from it at this time, but I should like to read from the latter part of an article published by the Searle' Grain Company, dealing with our western problems and what the tariff means to us. I quote:
There is one thing more to add. This assistance to the west is but temporary. The real problem is to secure markets for all the wheat the west is producing. These markets were once enjoyed by the west, and have been lost mainly because of high Canadian and other tariffs. The solution here is simply to lower Canadian tariffs; then will surpluses disappear, crops be sold, and prices rise. When these things occur western wheat growers will not need any further assistance either from the dominion or from the east.

In spite of the trade
arrangements with the United States our tariff is still of considerable proportions. Looking over the agreement with the United States, I picked out a few items in which the ordinary home-builder would be interested. I find that clothing still carries a duty of 30 to 35 per cent, and boots and shoes 30 per cent, and that the home-builder faces a duty of 27+ to 32+ per cent on furniture. Kitchen utensils carry a duty of 25 to 30 per cent and bathroom fixtures face a duty of 27+ to 30 per cent.
There is some justification for maintaining a tariff against foreign countries, but we are not justified in maintaining a high tariff against the mother country. Yesterday I got some recent figures from the Department of National Revenue. I am going to quote some of them, 71492-2184
but I will be as brief as possible. We enjoy a sheltered market in the old country and that is where we must sell our farm products. We have a free market there, and what is more, a tariff is imposed upon non-empire goods which affords a preference to empire commodities. It seems to me, therefore, that we have not played the game fairly with the mother country. Let me give some of these items.

Thus it will be seen that the tariff is still very high on goods coming from the old country into Canada.
I wish now to discuss briefly a subject in which the tariff does not seem to cut any figure. I am going to refer to farm machinery. I do not intend to discuss this question in detail because I have done so on a former occasion and others have gone into the subject. We had our parliamentary investigation two years ago. There was a United States probe at the same time and we have had a probe this year by the Saskatchewan legislature. All these investigations indicate that a combine exists in the manufacture of farm implements on this continent. The fact that when this government lowered the duty on farm implements from 25 per cent to 7+ per cent there was no reduction in the price but the reverse, was a defiance to parliament and an exploitation of the farmers of Canada, and this government should have taken action in the matter. Here was a chance for real reciprocity. Canadian manufacturers of farm implements enjoyed free
The Budget-Mr. Leader

access to United States markets, and this government should have insisted that United States machinery be allowed to enter Canada free. That action would have been justified for the reason that manufacturers of farm implements, in direct defiance of the government, increased their prices instead of lowering them when the tariff was lowered.

speechtext: Were not prices just as high in the United States?

Well, farmers in the United States were getting more for their produce. If we were getting ten or fifteen cents a bushel more for our grain, $3 a hundred pounds more for our cattle, a better price for our butter and so on, we could pay more for our machinery. The people of western Canada are deeply concerned about the price of farm implements. They are desperate. I know neighbours in my district, and there are people in the same position throughout western Canada, who are organizing in an effort to borrow machinery from one another because they have not the price to pay for new eqpipment.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on Hansard an article giving the views of the United Farmers of Manitoba. No doubt many of the ministers, and I presume every member from our province, have received copies of this memorandum. It gives the comments of four speakers who discussed this matter in the house some time ago, and in this case it seems that the first should be last, because they start out with myself. I quote:
Mr. Leader expressed the viewpoint of the farmers exactly when he said, "There are occasions-and they exist to-day. I believe, when it becomes the duty of a government to intervene if a great business organization takes advantage of its power to oppress its workers or to exploit the consumer."
Mr. Gardiner said, "I found that a binder that cost $295 a year ago would cost me $322 to-day. This is an increase of $27 between the time this committee first presented this report to the house and the present time."-"The industry has paid no attention to the complaints of farmers and the warnings of the committee. If they persist in this course action should be taken which they would fully understand and appreciate. Agriculture, which is the greatest primary industry in Canada, refuses to be bled any longer by half a dozen manufacturing plants which give as their only real reason the fact that they are employing 4,159 men."
Mr. Weir said, "The companies themselves, when being cross-examined by counsel for the committee, admitted that they could not justify their price increases by increase in the cost of production as regards raw materials, or any of the other items which enter into it, prior to 1930."
JMr. Leader.]
Then it quotes one of the oldest members of the house, a gentleman who enjoys the respect of all more than any other member, the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell).
Mr. Motherwell said, "The Minister of Agriculture issued a clarion call-for a lower price of farm implements, or at any rate a price not accentuated by reason of tariffs. If we are not to get it by reduction of tariffs then we must get it somehow. That was the philosophy of the minister's statement."

speechtext: What is the hon. member reading from?

From a memorandum sent out by the United Farmers of Manitoba. It closes with this comment:
Such emphatic statements as these naturally supported the growing assurance in the minds of the western farmers that practical measures would follow-. However, the session of 1938 closed and nothing was done.
And still another session is passing into the great beyond and no action has been taken. Let me assure the house that the Manitoba members did everything in their power to have the government take action in the matter. We went so far as to prepare a petition which in due course was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by the chief of our group, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). I had better read the petition:
Resolved that after an exhaustive study of the evidence submitted to the special committee of the house which inquired into the high price of agricultural implements, and in consequence of the full debate which took place relative to the concurrence of the special committee's report, we tihe following members of parlia ment and supporters of the Liberal party do hereby request that all customs duties be removed from farm implements and parts. Also that cream separators be placed on t'he free list as previous to 1932. We do request that the implement companies should have a drawback on all imported materials included in such implements.
That was signed by thirteen Liberal members from Manitoba, being, I think, all the Liberal members except the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar).
Now I have the letter that the Prime Minister sent to the hon. member for Marquette in acknowledging this petition. I quote:
Dear Mr. Glen,

I have noted the representations contained in t'he resolution, and shall not fail to see that they receive the careful consideration of the government as a whole.

speechtext:
The government has not taken adequate action; that is what I am complaining of, and that is what our people in western Canada are complaining of. I come from those people; I know what they are thinking, what they are telling me, and I tell them just what I am telling the house to-night.
Let me now give the personnel of the directorate of the Massey-Harris Company. I went to the trouble of digging this up, I believe it was two years ago, and in looking over my files found that I still had it. I find that none of the men who invented this machinery and brought it to its present standard is included in the directorate. No doubt they received considerable money when they left the company, and I do not think there is any one in Canada who begrudges these men any money they made out of that business; they worked hard for it. But at the present time who controls the Massey-Harris Company? Financiers who never did anything to build the machinery or bring it to its present state of development. Here are the names: T. A. Russell, president; J. S. Duncan, Toronto, vice-president; G. W. McLaughlin, Oshawa; E. R. Wood, Toronto; J. H. Gundy, Toronto; Frank P. Jones, Montreal; J. F. Lash, K.C., Toronto; Frederick K. Morrow, Toronto; J. A. Kilpatrick, Toronto; W. H. Moore, Toronto; G. W. Allan, K.C., Winnipeg.
Looking over the records of these gentlemen, I find some of them are directors in at least twenty-three companies; they are
men of big business. They control the tobacco industry, gold mines, oil fields, banks, grain companies, milling companies, cement companies, lumber mill, insurance, airports and mortgage companies, power companies-Beau-harnois, that name sounds rather familiar- chain stores, hockey rinks, steel companies and paper mills. What chance has the farmer of Canada with a directorate such as that? Mil-linaires who will close their factories when they cannot sell the goods, and who, instead of bringing down prices and selling reasonably, discharge their workmen and force them on relief for the people of Canada to support.
I have now come to a very important part of my remarks. I have to tell the house that it will be my duty to vote against the budget.

With these people I will pool my resources, hoping that by united action we can effect relief measures that will restore our purchasing power, reduce our unemployment, and strengthen our faith in God.
In addressing this letter to the electorate it is not my intention to detail a general policy, but there is one particular industry that requires a new deal. The great agricultural industry must be rehabilitated, and placed upon a more permanent foundation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to join with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) in expressing pleasure at the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has recovered his health and was able to deliver a most depressing budget without any apparent ill effects on him physically.
From the debate yesterday one would judge hon. members would have to conform to some new rules with respect to the budget debate, and would not be given the usual latitude customary when discussing the budget. When referring to certain bills on the order paper two hon. members were ruled out of order. After what happened this afternoon when the house met, it would seem that those two bills are to be revamped and rewritten to such an extent that when they appear again we may not be able to recognize them, and for that reason I do not propose to refer to them to-night. No doubt in respect of one the ante will be raised, as was indicated by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when referring to the bill of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). I just wonder why the Minister of Agriculture has to do

The Budget-Mr. Perley
most of the announcing for the Department of Trade and Commerce. However, we shall see the bills when they come down.
May I congratulate the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) upon the manner in which they have expressed themselves. They have had the courage of their convictions, and I wish there were more like them in the house. I have seldom known of a speech made in the house that has brought about such quick results as did the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Humboldt. We saw the results this afternoon when the ante was raised. I would say to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that if he had directed the resolution he read to us respecting agricultural implements in the west to the right place, rather than addressing it to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-if he had directed it to the Minister of Agriculture-he might have obtained some results. I say that because the Minister of Agriculture yielded to the committee that came down from the west and, as I say, he might have had some little influence in the cabinet and have brought about results.
Last night I was interested in the description by the hon. member for Humboldt of the different types or stripes of Tories. I wish he had described his own particular type to the house. However, he need not come over to this side of the house to describe Tories; there are so many peculiar types of Liberals on his own side it would take most of a forty minute speech to describe them. Had I the time at my disposal to-night I would take great pleasure in doing so, and I would begin with the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar).

I have a clear record of straight Conservatism, and I am not ashamed of the Conservative party. I have supported it throughout. I am not a wobbler like the Minister of Mines and Resources. Naturally, as a westerner I looked in the budget for something for the west, something to encourage western producers, but I failed to find anything. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said, the budget was a blank. It is a " do-nothing " budget by a " do-nothing " government. I recall the optimistic budgets delivered by the Minister
of Finance in 1937 and 1938. I recall the broadcast on the night of the election by the Prime Minister when he promised he would abolish poverty, adversity, and so on, and painted a wonderful picture. Now, after four years, nothing is done.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have only to wait and hope, so far as the budget is concerned. Nothing permanent for the producer is outlined, nor is there anything for the consumer. There is no reduction in taxation, and no indication that the government intends to take any action towards bringing about lower prices of implements of production, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. There was no indication that the government would bring the prices of those implements of production to a level comparable with the prices received by the producer for the product of his effort.
And how about the iniquitous sales tax? How about the sugar tax? A ten per cent reduction in the former would mean a saving of about 815,000,000 in what the consumer has to pay.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who put on the sugar tax?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will tell the hon. member about that. Oh, how in 1934 did we hear the wails from this side of the house! I can remember the hon. member for North Battle-ford (Mr. McIntosh) and the hon. membei for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) wailing about the sugar tax. When we had to increase the sales tax in a case of emergency to save this dominion, how they wailed about it! What hapened in the campaign of 1935? One would think from their speeches we would have a reduction. But now, when they come back they are prepared to swallow the sales tax when it is raised to 8 per cent, and the sugar tax remains.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did you do anything?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We took off one cent. You people were going to reduce it altogether, but you did not. The Minister of Finance was hopeful for next year, but with conditions as we know them to be and this government sitting idly by, especially during the last year, doing nothing, what may we expect? Surely we know. Is it any wonder that we have leadership leagues being formed when this government has not given the leadership the Canadian people desire and demand?
The budget stressed the importance of external trade and exports, but the figures of the Minister of Finance were shattered when the hon. member for York South (Mr. The Budget-Mr. Perley

Lawson) gave figures showing exports decreasing and imports not decreasing in comparison with the decrease in exports. We are heading toward an adverse trade balance. Why not investigate our internal trade? How many people know the value of our internal or domestic trade? How many people know what it amounts to or what it means to Canada? Ninety-five per cent of our natural agricultural products and 30 per cent of our wheat are consumed in Canada. The Liberal party stresses the importance of external trade. That trade is valuable along certain lines; but if it tends to increase unemployment in our country, if it becomes a question of trading Canada's raw products for the manufactured goods of other nations, then it is no good. On the other hand, domestic trade would tend to relieve the unemployment situation and increase employment. I would double the price of our agricultural products. It would then be found that unemployment would start to disappear. What would it amount to if the price of a cowhide, for instance, were doubled? How much would it increase the price of a pair of boots?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did you not do it when you were in office for five years?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I ask the hon. member
not to interrupt the hon. member who is speaking.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Leaving the local conditions of drought and crop damage aside for the moment, generally a nation-wide depression is accompanied by a great decrease in the price of farm products, while prices of secondary products remain almost stationary and certainly do not go any lower. I was referring to the possibility of increasing the price of cowhides or wool. If those prices were doubled, what would it mean to the cost of a pair of boots or a suit of underwear? If the price paid for a bushel of wheat were doubled, what would it mean to the price of a loaf of bread?
A commission investigated the baking industry a few years ago, and it was shown conclusively that there was no great difference in the price of a loaf of bread when wheat was selling at 70 cents a bushel or $1.60 a bushel. We are going round in a vicious circle. We have more relief, and this means higher taxes. Higher taxes mean higher costs of production. Higher costs of production mean a loss of trade, both external and internal. Loss of trade means more unemployment. More unemployment means more taxes. Thus we go round and round the vicious circle. I suggest to the government that they should employ such measures as would make that circle

a beneficial one. Double the prices for our agricultural and natural products and the result would be a beneficial circle.

The hon. member suggests
that the government should take action to double the prices of commodities produced on the farm. Would he tell the house just how he would do that?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the minister will just
sit quietly in patience for a little while I will try to explain. Better prices for our farm products would mean vastly increased purchasing power for half our population. An increased purchasing power would mean that more goods would be purchased. When more goods are purchased it means there would be increased employment at better wages. There would also be increased revenues for the government. I want to say here that the Bennett government directed its efforts toward increasing the prices of farm products. The measures introduced by the Minister of Agriculture will not increase by very much the prices of our agricultural production. The initial guaranteed price which he has suggested of 60 cents a bushel at Fort William is the lowest in practically fifty years and it will not tend to bring about the conditions which I have suggested. I do not think it will go very far in reversing the circle about which I have spoken. Courageous action on the part of the government in developing our natural resources and industry would go a long way toward relieving unemployment. If the price of wheat were set at a reasonable figure, say 87 cents a bushel or over, for a period of years you would be able to employ 200,000 more men on our Canadian farms annually.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We had a surplus in 1935
which disappeared in the world's markets. The Minister of Finance charged big business with timidity, but I do not see that this government has displayed any great courage or leadership. There are not many changes in the tariff under the budget because most of these occurred in connection with the trade agreement. Time alone will tell what the results will be, so I shall not deal with this phase of the matter just now. I should like to ask, where were the western Liberals, other than the two

The Budget-Mr. Perley
I have mentioned, when the budget was being prepared? What influence were they exerting upon tne government to carry out the policies which were promised to the people of western Canada? Only the hon. member for Humboldt and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie have taken the proper stand.
The minister mentioned the relief that has been given to the western provinces over a period of years. This amounts to $100,000,000 odd and I want to say that we appreciate it. However, when relief is necessary it should be given, but as relief. This relief would have meant much more to those needing it if it had been distributed in the proper manner. The administration of relief in Saskatchewan is a disgrace to this dominion. The administration of relief in that province has been so bad that its defects are quite apparent. The whole matter should be investigated, and if there is a change in government, which it is quite apparent there is going to be, the administration of relief in Saskatchewan will be sifted to the bottom.
Many matters of importance were referred to casually by the minister when he was delivering his budget speech, but time will not permit me to discuss them at this moment. They have been discussed more or less pro and con during this session, but with very little result.
The problem is the government's, and it is their responsibility. The Canadian people will	give their judgment at the first
opportunity. In computing the budget deficit for the fiscal year ending March 31 last at $55,000,000, the minister put the loss in connection with the operation last year of the wheat board at $25,000,000, but he did not say what it would be this year. No one knows that. For the next fiscal year the minister predicted a $60,000,000 deficit, again leaving out any losses in connection with wheat. Even this deficit figure is predicated upon an improvement in business conditions, which is not apparent. No provision is made in the budget for financing the pre-election agricultural measure recently introduced by the Minister of Agriculture in particular, and no one knows what it will involve. I shall not hazard a guess. But we know that this and other measures will be presented, and we know from what happened to-day that they will be rushed through the house in the dying days of the session, without any opportunity for proper consideration because there will be no time. Bill No. 62, not a very contentious measure, has been before the agriculture committee for I do not know how many sittings, and we are not through with 71492-219
it yet. If all the agricultural bills go to the agriculture committee it is doubtful if we could be through before August.
Coming back to the figure of $48,000,000, which has been referred to from time to time by the Minister of Agriculture as the loss on wheat, I charge that this government's policy was responsible for the greater part of that loss-the policy which they commenced in August of last year, the policy which they pursued of throwing huge quantities of wheat on the market, the selling policy, which they announced to the world. These policies, I charge, are responsible for more than half of that loss. Another part of the loss is accounted for in the carrying and storage charges allowed by private agreement to the grain companies. I wish I had time to deal with that feature to-night, but I may do so when the legislation is before the house. It represents a straight gift of five million dollars to the elevator companies in carrying or storage charges. They are making a service charge of one cent a bushel for performing no service whatsoever, and when the proper time comes, I have figures to substantiate my statement.
We shall not have time in the dying days of the session to give proper consideration to these very important bills. I know what happened, for example, the other day, when the second reading of Bill No. 104 was called, which the minister moved to refer to a committee, when not a single member had seen the bill at the time its second reading was moved. It had not even been printed. It was distributed in the house only five minutes after the minister made his motion. What a farce the whole thing is I Members are asked to consent to referring a 'bill to a committee when they have not even seen it.
Much has been said about the assistance that has been given to agriculture and the wheat producer. I want to say that the total assistance given to agriculture and the wheat producers in the seven years from 1930 to August 1, 1938, amounts to less than $22,000,000. I refer hon. members to the reports of the wheat board for 1937 and 1938, which are available to us all. The costs to date for assistance to agriculture and the wheat producers would be, first, the five cent bonus given by the Bennett government, amounting to $12,000,000; next, the adjustment with respect to the pools in 1935, of $6,500,000; and the net loss on the wheat board's 1935 and stabilization operations of $2,954,000, or a total of $21,454,000. That is apart from the 1938 crop, and it remains to be seen what it will be. Other exporting and importing countries have assisted their producers over

The Budget-Mr. Perley

the same period to the amount of four billion dollars, so Canada is not doing anything special in assisting the wheat producer as she has done. I take the position that there was no reason for a loss to be taken this year, and I may have an opportunity to discuss that when the bill is before us.
I desire to place on Hansard a weekly statement of the Canadian wheat board at the close of business August 13, 1938, and a
report of the wheat board covering the period from December 2, 1935, to May 29, 1937.

Grave alarm was felt in government and other quarters over the report last week from London that the United States is seeking to negotiate a barter deal with Great Britain in wheat and cotton and to dispose of one hundred million bushels of her wheat in the British market. After the signing of the Canada-United States treaty in Washington, the United States sold some thirty million bushels of wheat to Great Britain, and the sale of an additional one hundred million bushels of United States wheat would virtually shut Canada out of the British market. British imports of wheat last year from all countries totalled 190,000,000 bushels. After the Prime Minister of this country signed the new trade agreement at Washington, the government here issued a statement to the effect that the giving up by Canada of the 6 cent preference on wheat in the British market meant no sacrifice because the preference was of no benefit to this country. But the Washington government, on the other hand, issued a statement claiming that the removal of the 6 cent preference for Canadian wheat would restore United States wheat to its old position in the British market at the expense of the Canadian wheat grower. The recently reported barter deal negotiations are designed to make that claim good.
In the next five years we shall see a vast change in production and marketing methods. A committee of the international conference that was held in London is now working on a plan for a five-year quota on production and marketing. Undoubtedly great changes will be made in the next few years.
I should have liked to devote a little time to the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), but the hon. member for Humboldt and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie have handled that member so well that I shall waste little time to-night on his speech. He made some important statements with respect to the tariff. The only question I would be inclined to ask him would be, where were he and some other low-tariff members opposite when certain things were 71492-219i
happening? He also made a statement with respect to farm implements. I recall the statement he made in 1936 when he was moving for a committee to investigate the farm implement industry. I recall also the statement which the Minister of Agriculture made just before the Saskatchewan elections in 1934, warning the implement companies as to what might happen if they did not do thus and so. Why was not action taken along the lines suggested by the minister?
It is interesting to note the trend of business in Canada during the last two years. Wholesale prices in Canada have continued to sag, and probably will go lower. The drop in the price of raw materials has been substantially more severe than the decline in the price of manufactured goods. The slump in prices of Canadian farm products was about 25 per cent in the last two years, while the drop in prices of manufactured articles was only 8-8 per cent. There are only two ways in which this situation can be corrected. The price of manufactured goods must fall, or the price of primary products and raw materials must rise. Our exports of raw or unmanufactured goods are larger than our exports of manufactured goods. Our imports are chiefly manufactured goods. A comparison of prices of Canadian imports with export prices of our raw or unmanufactured products reveals one of the basic troubles which are holding back recovery.
There have been a number of rumours round the corridors of this building that protest meetings have been held by certain members respecting certain legislation, hole-in-the-comer meetings, I would suggest; and I protest against any minister of the crown making important statements with respect to changes of policy in impending legislation at hole-in-the-corner meetings with a few members and considering what will be the political effect of such changes.
The Minister of Agriculture made a visit to the west. He also made an evening broadcast, so he had many listeners, but he evi-
The Budget-Mr. Perley

dently gave them a headache, because the next morning they immediately started to get out a petition, which was signed by many thousands of farmers, protesting against the legislation which he had forecast in his address. It brought about delegations from the west to Ottawa to protest further. I understand that there was considerable bargaining and bartering when the Minister of Agriculture tried to make a deal with the premier of Manitoba whereby, if that premier would assist in discouraging pressure to be brought to bear on the government for measures to be referred to the committee on agriculture rather than have them go through the house, certain things would happen; for instance, Bill No. 63 would be withdrawn or left on the order paper. I object to that sort of thing. Once that kind of thing takes place, the whole marketing problem becomes a political football.
Many hon. members from the west have received petitions. I received one, which has 6,000 names on it, from my own constituency. A letter attached to one section of the petition was to the effect that it was not a political move; the writer had heard it charged that it was a political effort; he was sixty-four years of age and had ridden round on horseback getting people to sign the petition.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) made mention of certain resolutions passed at a Liberal meeting in the constituency of Qu'Appelle. I have a record of those resolutions, and I say that no greater condemnation of this government could be offered than the resolutions passed at that meeting; one, calling upon the government to take immediate action to reduce the cost of agricultural implements; another, asking the government to set a price of 80 cents on wheat; and another strongly worded resolution asking the federal authorities immediately to evolve some plan to create employment with a view of relieving the depression and the relief situation in Canada. Surely that is evidence of dissatisfaction and of condemnation of the government.

I wish to recall something else that happened in our province. During the campaign of 1934 a copy of a little pamphlet was put in practically every cream-can at the railway stations when it was being returned to the farmer. It was something like this: "Dollar wheat will pay your taxes, and pay for the licence for your automobile, and your gasoline. Dollar wheat will pay your grocery bills, and buy boots and shoes and clothing for your wife and kiddies. Vote Liberal." That is all it said. The people did vote Liberal. Have they got dollar wheat? The babies are still going barefoot, and we have the promise of 60-cent wheat.
Here is another one. During the campaign of 1935 another pamphlet was issued by the ton. Some hon. members received thousands of copies, and every Liberal member in this house saw them during the campaign. They were used against me. This pamphlet stated:
Secretary of State Cahan announced at a meeting last night in Montreal that the cabinet had fixed the price of 874 cents for the 1935-36 year. (This shows the cabinet, not Mr. Bennett, fixed the price.) You should receive 10 cents more a bushel for your wheat. Liberal association, Saskatchewan.
And then followed the name of the publisher. The Minister of Agriculture admitted that he was responsible for the issuing of that pamphlet, which was widely circulated. Now what have we? Well, we have nothing like the 974 cent wheat which was suggested there. They offer 60 cent wheat.
Now. Mr. Speaker, this is the place for constructive suggestions. I have a resolution which was put on the order paper on January 12, but which will die, like many others; it will never be reached. However, I have a constructive suggestion to offer now, and it is to this effect. I have made a study of this wheat marketing problem to as great an extent, perhaps, as any hon. member. I have been associated with the subject for a number of years. I believe that we should take a courageous position, that we can give the farmer some sense of security and some relief if a fixed minimum price is set for a number of years. I would suggest, sir, that from the western committee set up by what is usually called the Bracken conference there should be selected a smaller committee, representative of all interests in Canada, and that they should start to work along lines similar to those on which they have been working, and devise a scheme for a fixed minimum price for a number of years.

I make that suggestion
for this reason. The one cent added each month is practically the amount of the interest and the carrying charges on wheat, namely one cent a month, or one-thirtieth of a cent a day. It would encourage the farmer to hold his wheat on the farm, where it should be stored, and the cent a month would pay him exactly what the board is paying to elevator companies to carry the wheat once it is delivered to the board. Thereby the man would be assisted to carry his wheat and keep it out of the show window and out of the visible supply. That does not affect the man who cannot hold his wheat back, or all of it, because it does not affect the initial price; it is giving to the man who holds back his wheat only what the government is now giving to the elevator companies to hold the wheat. It would not cost the government any more. Further, I would issue participation certificates, and if the wheat was sold for more than the average I would set up a reserve fund. That is only business.
Further-and this is important-I would then set the domestic price of all wheat in Canada, the price of all wheat milled in the country for domestic purposes, at $1.20 a bushel, and I would regulate the price of flour, with the result that bread could be regulated, and it would not cost the consumer another cent a loaf. It would take sixty millions or more out of our export wheat, out of the visible supply, and that would be nothing more than what should be done. This is done in Australia and in other countries to a far greater extent than I suggest. The setting of a domestic price for all wheat used in Canada is a business proposition to which we shall come, and $1.20 a bushel is my suggestion. I wish I had time to elaborate this idea. I
The Budget-Mr. Perley

made this suggestion on the strength of the Turgeon commission's report, at page 23 of which is given the average price for the last forty-eight years. For the eighteen years prior to the war the average price was 91f cents; and for the eighteen years following the war the average price was S1.15J, and for the thirty-six years outside the war period the average was $1.03i, which is about five cents more than the Liberals suggested that the fixed price should be in 1935.
I am an optimist in this respect. I believe that history will repeat itself. In 1932 we had the greatest surplus in the world's market, and twice as much of a carry-over as we shall have this year. Under marketing conditions similar to those that prevail to-day, the Bennett government in 1935 set the price at S7J cents. And they were not wrong in doing so. All the wheat handled from 1930 to August, 1938, has not cost the country anything at all. The west has made a real contribution to confederation and has played its part. This is a national economic problem and must be met with courage by the government; and if this government does not grapple with the problem another government will come in that will. I simply put forward a business proposition for the consideration of the house. If the members from western Canada had the courage of their conviction; if they came here fully alive to their responsibility, to present to parliament what they know that their electors conceive to be the right thing for them to do, they would endorse the plan I propose. lVe want more men of the type of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.

This is the fourth session of the present parliament. I have sat through every session, and this is the first time I have attempted to trespass on the patience of the house. I believe I can advance fairly good reasons why I have remained so reticent. One is that I am penurious in bestowing compliments unless there is justification for it, and I am not prone to criticize unless I can take into consideration the various elements that enter into a discussion. Another valid reason may be, and it is a good, sane one, which I believe will have the approval of every member of the house, that I am weary listening to the superb mediocrity of ninety-five per cent of the speeches delivered here. I am
jMr. Perley.]
fully aware that any remarks of mine, regardless of the occasion, will gravitate toward that classification.
Needless to say I am not at all satisfied with the progress that the present government have made. I believe they could have done a great deal better, and being under that impression I sometimes wonder whether the Conservative party, had they been in office during the last four years, would have done as well as the present government, or, if one of the two expiring parties, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the Social Credit party, had been in office, what progress they would have made in the last three or four years. After giving the matter due and careful consideration, I have arrived at the irresistible conclusion that, regardless of the shortcomings of this government, it is, after all, the most progressive, most alert, and most democratic party we have in this house.
Let us take these parties in the order in which I have referred to them. We will take first the Conservative party-and right here let me extend my sincere felicitations to the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon his appointment to the leadership of his party. It is my candid opinion, however, that as long as he has the honour of a seat in this house he will be sitting to the left of the Speaker. In that respect, I am sure that he will find consolation in the fact that this is a sad and cruel world-we never strew flowers on a man's grave until after he is dead. Shortly after his appointment as leader of his party he made a tour of the country. He visited western Canada and made speeches in Saskatchewan, the province in which I live. I listened to him when he spoke in Moose Jaw. I was 200 miles away, sitting in my home, and I listened to him over the radio. I had not been listening very long when I came to the conclusion that it was a good thing his party was not in office at the present time. He discussed the tariff, and he discussed it in such a manner that, if I did not know to what religious denomination he belonged, I would have said he was a spiritualist. Everything that he said about the tariff was veiled in such opaque nebulosity that I could not tell where he stood on the tariff. It was hard to say whether he was coming or going. If that was his attitude on the tariff-
